comments.text: Good article! Two things popped into my head when reading it. First the talk "Programming with Hand Tools" by Tim Edwald[0]. It's a very cool, entertaining talk with emphasis on the craftsmanship side of things and provokes thinking about which parts to automate (or maybe abstract away) and which parts to craft by hand when we're building stuff. Aside: also reminds me of Casey Muratori's Handmade Hero project [1]. He is a strong advocate for structuring things bottom up and building them ourselves. [0] [VIDEO] [1] [LINK] --- Secondly when reading this: > Regardless, the basic idea is that companies are often faced with the decision of doing N units of shitty work or far fewer than N units of great work. This is obviously oversimplified, but there is an important point that wants to emerge from this line of thought. As someone who grew up on open source, standardized technologies and the Web, I have been empowered to build a livelihood on Web development, mostly "self-taught" (or rather self-directed). All of this Web stuff is very accessible and gives you actual _leverage_. You can build something useful very quickly and the community around it is happy to share so much knowledge and work. I'm _very_ thankful for that. But I think as the wider web development community we're losing sight of what that essence is. comments.author: adityaathalye
comments.why_zh: 借家具制作和 Clojure 谈自动化对工作的影响
comments.quote_zh: 他也把它和木工联系了起来。
comments.text_zh: Tim Ewald 在他 2013 年 Clojure/conj 的这场演讲中为“Programming with Hand Tools”站台辩护。他也把它和木工联系了起来。[视频] 摘要：在人类历史的大部分时间里，家具都是靠手工、用一小组简单工具做出来的。这种方式让你与工作、与自己的付出和成果之间建立起一种极其直接的联系。随着机床的兴起，这一切改变了：生产效率更高了，但也深刻地改变了被制造出来的东西，以及我们如何看待制造这件事。这场演讲探讨自动化对我们工作的影响——这一点对软件和对家具同样适用，尤其是现在，我们又一次借助 Clojure，用一小组简单工具来造东西。
comments.text: Time Ewald makes a case for "Programming with Hand Tools" in this talk he gave at Clojure/conj 2013. He too makes a connection with wood working. [VIDEO] Summary: For most of human history, furniture was built by hand using a small set of simple tools. This approach connects you in a profoundly direct way to the work, your effort to the result. This changed with the rise of machine tools, which made production more efficient but also altered what's made and how we think about making it in in a profound way. This talk explores the effects of automation on our work, which is as relevant to software as it is to furniture, especially now that once again, with Clojure, we are building things using a small set of simple tools.

comments.text_zh: 有意思的是，即便作为一个非常懂 js、已经用了十年（其实更久！）的人，生态系统的爆发还是让我吃惊。一年多前我离开 Web 代理公司的岗位，和一个朋友做我的创业项目，所以一直处于相对孤立的开发状态（大量用 python 和 js，但不太跟最新趋势）。最近回来帮一个项目，不得不花一天研究所有新工具。尤其是包管理相关的 bower、grunt、yeoman、node、npm 等等。一年前，一个 js 库通常就是一个 js 或 min.js 文件交付。现在它周围有一整套体系；如今 github 上每个项目似乎都包含针对各个不同包管理器的配置。甚至还有一个 vagrant 文件，让你能在全新的 vm 上把一切跑起来。就连给项目添加 bootstrap 这样简单的事，第一眼看也不是完全显然。代码放哪里？怎么编译才能不碰 vendor src 本身，同时又能自定义它，等等。我有一套适合自己的方法，但当初也得折腾一会儿才弄明白怎么让它满足我的需求。一旦过了那个阶段，我对当时的状况真的很满意。现在 JS 库安装和版本控制都很好很方便，到目前为止 bower 的依赖管理对我来说效果很好。Grunt 让开发中的自动化部分变得舒服、集中且容易共享。总而言之，这真的是一个非常好的
comments.text: It's funny, even as someone who knows js really well, having worked with it for a decade (actually, longer!), the explosion in the ecosystem took me by surprise. I left my web agency role over a year ago to work on my start up with a friend so I've been in relative developmental isolation (lots of python and js, not so much keeping up with the latest trends). I came back to help out on a project recently and had to spend a day researching all the new tools. Particularly around package management, bower, grunt, yeoman, node, npm etc. A year ago a js lib was generally delivered as a js or min.js file. Now there's the whole system to sit around it; every project on github now seems to include the config for each of the different package managers. Even a vagrant file so you can get it all up and running on a brand new vm. Something as simple as adding bootstrap to a project. It's not totally obvious when you first look at it. Where does the code go? How do you compile it in such a way that you don't touch the vendor src itself but you can customise it etc. I have a method that works for me, but I had to play around a little to figure out how to fit it to my needs. Once I got through that stage I was really happy with where things were at. JS libs are nice and easy to install and version control now, dependency management with bower has worked really well for me so far. comments.text_zh: “wat”是识别问题的良好第一步。但我看到的是，人们卡在“wat”上，不再往前走。人们宁愿赢一场争论，也不愿推进知识与实践。程序员有很多自我。与此同时，人们可以学会欣赏并使用 javascript 的优势。它可以相当有趣、解放且有用。就我的个人经验而言，我每天写 javascript，却没有遇到这些疯狂的问题。我也在做一个大型应用，我构建的框架是自定义的。我把它比作以 C++、Unix 和 bash 为基础。是的，你可以说这些工具很烂，然后花时间为一款新工具做创建、营销和社区建设。或者你可以迭代并改进这些现有工具。没有错误答案。你想达成什么？ > 寿司刀不会因为米饭来自不同产地就决定割伤你。这个类比似乎有点牵强。愿意解释一下吗？Javascript 能处理不同 locale。有很多国际网站使用 javascript。而且，javascript 并不会“决定”在你的程序里制造 bug。是你误用工具制造了那个 bug。如果你承担一些责任并改进自己的实践，你会走得更远。 > 而且我猜，大多数工匠，除了在仪式和传统之外，都会希望自己的工具缺点更少。我同意这一点。通常改进是迭代式的。你可以用激光切割机（它不需要磨）来切寿司，但那也会把寿司烧焦。这里
comments.text: The "wat" is a good first step in identifying problems. However, I see is people getting stuck on "wat" and not moving forward. People would rather win an argument than advance knowledge & the practice. Lot's of ego, programmers have. In the mean time, one can learn to appreciate & use javascript strengths. It can be quite fun, liberating, & useful. Anecdotally, I have not run into these crazy issues, and I program in javascript everyday. I also have a large app and the framework I built is custom. I liken this to using C++, Unix, & bash as a base. Yes, you could say these tools suck and spend time creating, marketing, & community-building for a new tool. Or you can iterate & improve upon these existing tools. There's no wrong answer. What do you want to accomplish? > Sushi knives don't decide to cut you because the rice came from a different origin. That analogy seems like a stretch. Care to explain? Javascript works with different locales. There are many international websites that use javascript. Also, javascript does not "decide" to create a bug in your program. You create that bug by misusing the tool. You will get further if you take some responsibility and improve your practice. > And I'd guess that most craftsmen, outside of a ritual and tradition would love for their tools to have less disadvantages.
